text: We have already defined the degree of a node as the number of edges connected to it, thus
specifying if a node is more connected than another.
Looking closer, we can separate out the two components of a node's degrees into in-degree
and out-degree, which are the counts of the incident and the outgoing edges of a node,
respectively.
In the example graph, G has an in degree and out degree of 3, making the total degree equal
to 6. We first construct this degree table for each node. It is a simple procedure where
we count the number of nodes with degree 0, 1, 2 and so forth. The degree versus count
table is the degree histogram of the graph.
We can compare two graphs by computing the vector distance between them.
One simplistic measure is just the Euclidean distance.
For our case, the degree histogram based on comparison of the histograms find the graphs
to be very similar.
The more sophisticated methods are available, but are outside the scope of this course.
We can also compute histograms of just the in-degree or just the out-degree of the graph.
But perhaps more interesting is a joint two-dimensional histogram of a graph.
The colorful histogram of the graph can be interpreted here as follows.
The graph has a maximum in-degree of 3 and a maximum out-degree of 3.
This creates a two-dimensional histogram with 4 times 4 equal to 16 different joined values.
The actual value for any combination is computed from the graph and color-coded in the matrix.
For example, there is no node with in-degree 0 and out-degree 0.
So the lower left square of the graph has value 0 and color-coded glue.
On the other hand, there are two nodes with in-degree 3 and out-degree 3.
the top right corner has the value 2, which is 20% of the nodes, color coded as light green.
The 2D histogram provides an interesting insight. The nodes with more incident edges than outgoing
edges represent entities that take in more than they put out. In a social networking setting,
they represent members who are listeners. They receive a lot of posts, but send much
fewer posts. On the opposite side of the spectrum, there are talkers whose out degrees exceed
their in degrees. The entities that are in between may have both large values of in degree
and out degree.
These are communicators.
In this graph, there seems to be more talkers than listeners.
Not surprising though, my social media friends show similar statistics.
